title: Canonical writer, and prove the round trip
description:
Write a model back to disk in a canonical form, and prove it round-trips.

This is the item the whole format stands on. If it is wrong, every studio save
produces a diff nobody can review, and the tool has failed at its only job.

## Scope

- `src/model/write.ts`: a function returning a file's full text for any kind
  (table, note, group), and `writeModel(dir, model)` writing each object to its
  own file in the right directory. ADR 0005 has the layout.
- Canonical means fixed: key order, indentation, quoting style, where blank
  lines go, and a single trailing newline. Two people producing the same model
  produce byte-identical files.
- The prose body is written back exactly as it was read.
- Group membership is written on the member and never on the group, and group
  geometry is never written at all because it is computed. If the writer emits
  either, the merge story in ADR 0005 is broken.

## The two properties to hold

1. Parsing a serialised model gives back an equal model, for every model.
2. Serialising a parsed file gives back identical bytes, for every canonical
   file.

The second only holds for canonical input, and that is the point: a hand-written
file normalises on the first save and then never moves again. Write a test that
reads a deliberately untidy fixture, saves it twice, and asserts the second save
changed nothing.

## Watch out for

- A write that is not atomic loses a file. The studio writes on every drag.
  Write to a temporary file in the same directory and rename over the target: a
  partial write on a crash is a corrupted model, and the developer has git as
  their undo, which will not have the file yet.
- Never write a file that failed to parse. A model carrying a diagnostic for a
  table must leave that table's file alone rather than serialise whatever half
  model it managed to build.
- Do not write files you did not change. Writing all forty tables when one moved
  makes `git status` useless and destroys the reviewability the format exists
  for. Compare the rendered text with what is on disk and skip if equal. This
  matters most for a group drag, which moves every member at once: only the
  members that actually moved get written.
- YAML emitters love to reflow, fold long strings, and drop quotes they think
  are unnecessary. Any of those turn a stable file into a churning one. If the
  library fights you, emit the frontmatter yourself: it is a fixed set of keys.

## Evidence bar

Show the actual `git diff` from changing one column's type in a ten-table
fixture. It must be one line. Then show the diff from adding one table to a
group: it must be one line, in that table's file, and the group file must be
untouched. Paste both in the pull request.

## Out of scope

Validation (dbmd-12). The studio's calls to this (dbmd-30).

title: Model types and the reader
description:
Read a `db-model/` directory into a typed model in memory.

## The directory, per ADR 0005

```
db-model/
  _model.md          name, engine, prose about the model as a whole
  tables/*.md        kind: table
  notes/*.md         kind: note
  groups/*.md        kind: group
```

The directory decides the kind. The `kind:` key in the frontmatter is a
cross-check, and a file whose `kind` disagrees with its directory is a
diagnostic, never a silent reinterpretation.

## Scope

- `src/model/types.ts`: `Model`, `Table`, `Column`, `Index`, `Ref`, `Note`,
  `Group`. Exact shapes are yours; ADR 0003 and ADR 0005 have the fields.
- `src/model/read.ts`: `readModel(dir)` returns the model plus a list of
  diagnostics. It does not throw on a bad file; a bad file is a diagnostic with
  a path and a line, because the studio has to show that rather than crash.
- Two computed indexes, built once here because the studio, the validator and
  the exporter all want them: which tables point at a given table, and which
  tables are in a given group. Group membership is declared by the member with
  a `group` key and is never stored on the group.
- The markdown body after the frontmatter is kept as one opaque string, exactly
  as read, newline for newline. It is never parsed as markdown. For a note the
  body is the note.

## Watch out for

- YAML will silently do the wrong thing and look right. A key named `null` is a
  real key and depending on the parser it can arrive as a boolean. A column
  default of a quoted SQL string must survive with its quotes intact rather than
  arriving as a bare word. Pick a YAML parser that lets you see the raw scalar
  and its style, and write a test for both of those exact cases before you write
  anything else.
- YAML 1.1 booleans. A column typed `y` or `no` is unusual but `on` and `off`
  are not, and neither is a table named `on`. Every place a string is expected,
  assert it is a string and diagnose rather than coerce.
- CRLF. This repository normalises to LF on checkout and developers are on
  Windows. The body string must not gain or lose a carriage return on the way
  through, or every save produces a whole-file diff. There is a `.gitattributes`
  doing half of this; do not rely on it doing the other half.
- A frontmatter block that is absent, empty, or unterminated are three different
  diagnostics, and a file with no frontmatter at all is a plain markdown file
  that happens to be in the directory. Decide what that is and say so in code.
- A group key naming a group file that does not exist is a diagnostic, not a
  reason to invent the group.

## Evidence bar

A fixture directory with at least: a table with a composite primary key, a
column whose default is a quoted SQL string, a column named `null`, a table
whose prose body contains a fenced code block with three dashes inside it, a
file with broken YAML, a note, a group with two members, and a file in the wrong
directory for its kind. Report what `readModel` returned for the broken ones,
not that it did not throw.

## Out of scope

Writing (dbmd-11). Validating references (dbmd-12).
close_reason: Merged in PR #5. Reader verified against an orchestrator-written adversarial fixture, not the PR's own: null key, quoted SQL default, YAML-boolean-shaped names, byte-exact CRLF body through a fence containing three dashes, and the group not invented.

comments.author: Blake Hastings
comments.text:
Dispatched 2026-08-25, stopped by the owner before it reported.

What it left in its worktree: `yaml@^2.9.0` added to package.json and installed.
No commits, no source files, no tests. Nothing worth preserving, and nothing was
merged or pushed. `main` is untouched.

Not resumed and not finished by the orchestrator. The item is open and
unchanged, and the next dispatch starts clean.

One real finding came out of it anyway: agent worktrees are created at
`.claude/worktrees/` inside the repository, so every one of them shows up as
untracked in `git status` on `main`. Fixed separately.

comments.author: Blake Hastings
comments.text:
## Functionality

Drove the reader myself against a fixture I wrote, not the one in the PR, built
specifically to break the four claims this item stands on. Compiled `dist` and
called `readModel` directly.

- `null: false` arrives as `nullable: false`. The key named `null` survived.
- `default: "'pending'"` arrives as the nine characters `'pending'`, quotes
  intact. `default: "false"` arrives as the string `false`, not a boolean.
- A column named `on` arrives as the string `on`.
- `ref: other.id` resolves to `{ table: 'other', column: 'id' }`.
- `group: nope`, naming a group with no file, is kept on the table, produces
  `group-unknown`, and `groupMembers` has no `nope` key. The group is not
  invented, which is the ADR 0005 property.
- The body round-trips byte for byte. My fixture used CRLF throughout, a fenced
  SQL block containing a line of three dashes, trailing spaces, and no final
  newline. `onDisk.endsWith(body)` is true, the carriage returns are still
  there, and the fence did not terminate the frontmatter.

Line numbers are honest: `group: nope` is on line 20 of my file and the
diagnostic says 20. A missing `_model.md` warns with no line rather than a
fabricated one.

That is the item's central claim and it holds.

## Code

Read the reader. The kind dispatch, the field reader and the diagnostic
plumbing are one shape each rather than three, which is what keeps a 980-line
file legible. Reading map keys from the scalar's source text whenever a plain
scalar did not resolve to a string is a good single rule: it makes `null:`,
`on:` and a quoted `"null":` all behave, instead of three special cases.

Not storing the quoting style is right, and the PR gives the reason: ADR 0003
has the writer emit a canonical style, so remembering the input's style would
be remembering something the writer is going to discard.

**One defect, and it is one byte.** `test/model/read.test.ts` contains a literal
NUL at offset 1241, inside `customers?.body ?? '<NUL>'`, which was meant to be
`''`. Consequences, in order of how much they matter:

1. **Git classifies the file as binary.** `git diff --stat` reports
   `Bin 0 -> 16788 bytes`, so the largest test file in the pull request cannot
   be reviewed as a diff, now or in any future change to it. In a repository
   whose entire premise is that the diff is the review, that is the finding.
2. The assertion still behaves acceptably: if `customers` were undefined,
   `endsWith('\0')` is false and the test fails loudly.

CI is green and will stay green, which is exactly why this needed reading
rather than trusting.

## Architecture

ADR 0008 is a real record: it states the rule (diagnose, never coerce), names
what it costs, and its assumptions are the kind that would otherwise be
invisible, particularly the file name being the identity with `table:` as a
cross-check.

No entropy added. `src/import/`, `src/index.ts` and the concurrent agent's
surface were left alone as briefed. `package.json` gained exactly one
dependency with one transitive, and the PR says what it buys and what was
considered instead.

The report that YAML 1.1 booleans are unreachable through frontmatter is
reported as a finding rather than claimed as a fix, and the string assertions
are still in place regardless. That is the right way round.

## Verdict

Send back for the one byte. Everything else is ready to land.

title: The model on disk
description:
The model on disk, as ADR 0003 describes it: one markdown file per table under
`db-model/`, YAML frontmatter for structure, free markdown for the prose that
explains why the table exists.

Everything else in this project reads and writes through this layer. The CLI,
the studio and the importer are all clients of it, so getting the round-trip
right here is what stops every one of them producing noisy diffs.

Read `docs/architecture/decisions/0003-markdown-on-disk-is-the-model.md` before
opening any child of this epic. It carries the four requirements the format
exists to satisfy and the rejected alternatives, so an agent that skips it will
re-argue a settled question in a pull request.

title: One Diagnostic type, not two
description:
Two `Diagnostic` types, converged independently, now a parallel source of truth.

Found by the dbmd-10 agent reviewing its own rebase against dbmd-40's merged
work, which is the entropy question review lens 3 asks and the reason it is
asked.

## What is there now

`src/model/types.ts` and `src/import/diagnostics.ts` each define `Diagnostic`,
a `DiagnosticCode`, a `'error' | 'warning'` severity, and a code-unit sort
(`compareDiagnostics` / `byText` against `compareCodeUnits` / `sortDiagnostics`).
Two agents working in parallel, neither able to see the other, arrived at nearly
the same shape. That they converged is evidence the shape is right. That there
are two of them is the problem.

## The real divergences

- **`path` means different things.** In the model reader it is a filesystem path
  relative to the model directory, with an optional 1-based `line`. In the
  import contract it is a JSONPath rooted at `$`, with no line, because its input
  is a JSON document with no lines to point at. Both are correct for their own
  input, and `dbmd check --json` will eventually emit both.
- **Message style.** The import convention is one sentence with no trailing full
  stop. Several model messages end with one.

## Why this is worth an item rather than a refactor in passing

ADR 0006 makes diagnostic structure a public contract, because `--json` exposes
it. Unifying after that ships is a breaking change; unifying before it costs
nothing. So this wants doing before dbmd-21 (`dbmd check`), and dbmd-21 is what
would otherwise be forced to reconcile them at the point of printing.

## Watch out for

- **Do not force one `path` to mean the other.** A JSONPath and a file path with
  a line number are genuinely different things. The likely answer is a common
  `Diagnostic` with a discriminated location, not a lowest common denominator
  string that loses the line number.
- The severity type and the sort are the parts that should simply be shared.
  Two sorts that agree today will not agree forever.
- This touches `src/model/` and `src/import/` at once, so it cannot be
  dispatched alongside work in either.

## Evidence bar

One `Diagnostic` type imported by both. Show the `--json` shape a mixed run
would emit, with one diagnostic from each side in the same array, and say what a
consumer does to tell them apart.

title: The output contract, built once and enforced
description:
The output contract, built once and enforced.

ADR 0006's four rules, made into code that other commands cannot get wrong by
accident. Do this before there are four commands rather than after.

## Scope

- `src/cli/output.ts`: one place that owns writing. Data goes to stdout,
  narration goes to stderr, and a command that wants to print does it through
  here rather than through `console.log`.
- Colour on when stdout is a TTY, off otherwise, off when `NO_COLOR` is set in
  the environment, and `--no-color` to override the detection. No colour library:
  this is a handful of escape codes.
- `--json` handled once: same exit codes as the text form, JSON on stdout,
  nothing else on stdout.
- A deterministic sort helper, used by everything that emits a list.
- A lint rule or a test that fails on a bare `console.log` outside this module.
  That is the part that makes the contract hold in six months.

## Watch out for

- `console.log` writes to stdout and `console.error` writes to stderr, and it is
  extremely easy to narrate to stdout by habit. That single mistake breaks every
  pipe and every agent, and it is invisible in a terminal because both look the
  same on screen. The test is the only thing that catches it.
- Exit codes with `--json` are the classic bug: the command prints valid JSON
  describing three errors and exits 0 because printing worked.
- Windows terminals and escape codes. Verify colour detection on Windows and in
  a piped context on Windows, not just in one shell that happens to work.
- Do not add a `--quiet`. If narration is on stderr, quiet is `2>/dev/null` and
  the flag is a symptom of rule 1 having been broken somewhere.

## Evidence bar

For one real command, paste four runs: at a TTY, piped to `cat`, with `--json`
piped to a JSON parser, and with `NO_COLOR` set. Show the exit code in the
failing case for both the text and the JSON forms.

title: An example model that is the demo, the fixture and the test data
description:
An example model that is the demo, the fixture, and the test data.

One realistic model, committed, that does three jobs at once. That is the point:
three copies of a sample schema drift apart, and the one that goes stale is
always the one in the README.

## Scope

- `examples/shop/` : a small commerce model with maybe eight tables, real
  relationships, at least one composite primary key, one grouping box, and two
  sticky notes that say something a schema cannot.
- The prose in it is written properly. This is the file people will read to
  understand what the prose is for, so a table documented with "the orders
  table" teaches exactly the wrong lesson.
- `npm run dev` opens the studio on it, and the test suite uses it as a fixture.

## Watch out for

- It has to stay valid. Wire `dbmd check` on `examples/shop` into `npm run check`
  as soon as `dbmd check` exists, or this rots within a month.
- Resist making it big. Eight tables that each earn their place beats thirty that
  demonstrate a feature list, and the diagram has to be legible in a screenshot.
- Do not use a real company's schema, and do not use anything that looks like
  personal data.

## Watch out for the ordering

This is worth doing early even though the format is not finished, because it is
the fastest way to find out that the format is annoying to write by hand. If
writing this by hand is unpleasant, that is a finding about ADR 0003 and it
should be reported rather than worked around.

title: CONTRIBUTING and the path from clone to a running studio
description:
CONTRIBUTING.md, and the path from clone to a running studio.

## Scope

- `CONTRIBUTING.md`: prerequisites, `npm ci`, `npm run check`, and the one
  command that puts a real model on screen. Then the reading order for anyone
  about to change something: AGENTS.md, the decision records, and which ADR
  covers the area they are touching.
- A `npm run dev` script that starts the studio on the example model with an
  OS-assigned port, so a contributor's first successful command produces a
  picture rather than a passing test.
- Say plainly what this project will and will not accept. It does not generate
  DDL and does not connect to databases, and both of those are decisions rather
  than gaps, so a contributor should learn that before writing the PR.
- The decision-record habit, in three sentences: numbers are handed out, not
  taken, and `npm run check` fails a collision.

## Watch out for

- Do not document commands you have not run on a clean clone. The classic
  failure is instructions that work only because your machine already has
  something. Test from a fresh clone in a different directory.
- Windows. This is developed on Windows and most contributors will not be on it.
  Every command in the file has to work in both places or say which is which.
- Do not restate AGENTS.md. Link it. Two files describing the same conventions
  drift, and the one that drifts is always the one nobody runs.

## Evidence bar

Clone this repository into a fresh directory, follow your own file top to
bottom, and paste the terminal from the clone to the studio being open. If a
step needed something the file did not mention, that is the finding.

title: One CLI, three callers
description:
One CLI, three callers: a human, a pipeline, and an agent.

ADR 0006 is the contract. This epic is making it real and keeping it true.

The three callers want opposite things and a CLI designed for any one of them is
actively bad in the other two. A tool that prompts hangs a GitHub Actions job for
six hours. A tool whose output reorders between runs makes an agent think
something changed. A tool that mixes progress chatter into stdout cannot be
piped anywhere.

The rules are checkable rather than aspirational, which is the point: stdout is
data and stderr is narration, nothing ever prompts, everything that reports has
a JSON form, and the same input produces the same bytes.

Read `docs/architecture/decisions/0006-one-cli-three-callers.md` before opening
any child of this epic.

title: The repository a contributor can run
description:
The repository a contributor can understand and run.

This is an MIT-licensed open source project, which means the first experience
most people have of it is not the tool. It is this repository, arriving from a
link, on a machine that has nothing installed.

Two audiences, and they need different things:

- **Someone evaluating it.** They want to know what it is and whether it solves
  their problem, in under a minute, without cloning anything.
- **Someone contributing.** They want to get from clone to a running studio with
  a real model in front of them, in one command, and then to know where the
  decision they are about to argue with was already made.

The second one is what this epic is mostly about, because the first is the
README and that is dbmd-51.

The thing that makes this repository unusual is that it already writes its
decisions down. `docs/architecture/decisions/` is not overhead here, it is the
answer to most of what a new contributor will ask. What is missing is the path
that points them at it.

title: Notes and groups on the canvas
description:
Notes and groups on the canvas.

The part that makes this a diagram rather than a schema dump. ADR 0005 has the
format and the reasoning; read it before you start, particularly the section on
why a group has no coordinates.

## Scope

**Notes.** Create, move, resize, edit, delete. The body is markdown and it is
rendered, not shown raw, but editing is a plain textarea. A colour from a small
fixed palette, named rather than a hex value, so a diff says `color: amber` and
not `color: "#fbbf24"`.

**Groups.** Create with a label and a colour. A table joins or leaves a group
from the inspector, which writes one line in that table's file. The group box is
drawn as the bounding box of its members plus padding, computed on every render
and never stored. Dragging the group's header moves every member, and each
member's own layout line is what changes.

Groups render behind everything and notes render in front of the tables, because
a note is a person talking and a group is a region.

## Watch out for

- **A group must never acquire coordinates.** The temptation is to cache the
  bounding box for performance and then to write it "just this once" when
  somebody resizes. That is the failure mode ADR 0005 exists to prevent, and it
  turns into a file that can disagree with reality.
- Dragging a group is a multi-file write. Flush all of it on pointerup as one
  batch, and write only the members that actually moved.
- An empty group has no bounding box. Render something rather than nothing, or a
  group whose last member left vanishes and the user thinks they deleted it.
- Removing a table from the canvas that is a group's only member leaves an empty
  group, which the validator warns about. Do not silently delete the group.
- A note resize writes `w` and `h`. Debounce it like everything else, and snap to
  something coarse, or a drag produces a diff for every pixel.
- Group colours and note colours have to be legible in both light and dark. Pick
  the palette once, in one place, and do not let each component invent a shade.

## Evidence bar

Build a fixture with six tables, put three of them in a group, add two notes.
Then, in the studio: drag the group, and paste the `git diff`, which must be
three `layout` lines in three table files and nothing in the group file. Drag
one table out of the group and paste the diff, which must be one line in one
file. Include a screenshot of the canvas with the group box and the notes on it.

title: The inspector: columns, indexes, prose
description:
The inspector: edit a table's columns, indexes and prose.

## Scope

- Selecting a table opens a side panel.
- Edit the table name, and add, remove, reorder and edit columns: name, type,
  nullability, primary key, default, and `ref`.
- Add and remove indexes.
- Edit the markdown body in a plain textarea. It is text, not a rich editor.
- Every change writes through, debounced, like everything else.

## Watch out for

- Renaming a table must update every `ref` that points at it, or the rename
  silently breaks the model. That touches other files, which means other diffs;
  say so in the interface before doing it rather than after.
- A textarea will happily give you carriage returns on Windows. The body must
  reach disk with the same line endings it left with, or every prose edit is a
  whole-file diff.
- Typing in a field must not write a file per keystroke. Debounce, and do not
  reformat the field under the user's cursor while they are still in it.
- Removing a column that another table refs is a real decision. Warn, name the
  tables, and let it happen: this is a modelling tool and a broken ref is a
  diagnostic, not something to prevent.

## Evidence bar

Rename a table that two other tables point at, and paste the resulting
`git diff` across all three files. Then edit a prose body and show that the diff
is only the lines you typed.

title: The canvas: boxes, edges, pan, zoom, drag
description:
The canvas: table boxes, relationship edges, pan, zoom and drag.

## Scope

- Each table is an absolutely positioned element listing its columns, with the
  primary key and foreign keys marked.
- Each `ref` is an edge on one SVG overlay behind the boxes.
- Pan and zoom are a CSS transform on the container. Drag moves a box and writes
  the new `layout` through to disk, debounced.
- Positions come from `layout` in the frontmatter. A table without one is placed
  on a deterministic grid rather than at random.

## Watch out for

- Dragging with a CSS transform in play is the classic source of the box that
  jumps on mousedown or drifts from the cursor at zoom levels other than 1.
  Convert screen coordinates to model coordinates once, in one function, and use
  it everywhere. Test at zoom 0.5 and 2, not just at 1.
- Use pointer events, not mouse events, and capture the pointer. Without capture
  a fast drag that leaves the window leaves a box stuck to the cursor.
- Debounce writes, but flush on pointerup. A drag that ends and then never gets
  written because the tab lost focus is the one bug that makes a developer stop
  trusting write-through.
- Edges to and from the same pair of tables overlap. Two straight lines on top
  of each other read as one relationship, which is wrong in a way nobody
  notices. Offset them or curve them.

## Evidence bar

Open a fixture model with at least ten tables, drag three boxes, and paste the
`git diff`. It must touch exactly three files, one line each. Include a
screenshot of the canvas.

## Out of scope

Auto layout, multi-select and a minimap are all deliberately not in the MVP.
ADR 0004 says when to revisit that.

title: The studio server
description:
The studio server: loopback, ephemeral port, and it edits files.

## Scope

- `dbmd studio [--port N] [--no-open]`. Default port 0, meaning the OS picks;
  print the URL it actually bound to. Bind to 127.0.0.1 only.
- Serves the client bundle, built by esbuild as part of `npm run build`.
- `GET /api/model` returns the model plus diagnostics.
- `PATCH /api/table/:name` applies an edit and writes through, debounced a few
  hundred milliseconds so a drag is one write rather than sixty.
- `POST /api/table` and `DELETE /api/table/:name` for adding and removing.
- Every response says when the last write to disk landed, so the client can show
  it rather than guess.

## Watch out for

- Never write outside the model directory. A table renamed to `../../etc/x` is a
  path traversal, and this server writes files on behalf of a web page. Resolve
  every path and assert it is still inside the model root before writing. This
  is the one security property this tool has and it is worth a test that tries.
- Bind to loopback explicitly. `server.listen(port)` alone listens on all
  interfaces, and this is somebody's laptop on a coffee shop network.
- Never write a file that failed to parse, and never write a file you did not
  change (dbmd-11 has both).
- `--port 0` is not a nicety. Several agent worktrees run this at once, and a
  fixed default makes them collide silently with whichever started first.
- Do not add an HTTP framework. `node:http` serves four routes and a static
  directory in under a hundred lines, and install time is a feature here.

## Evidence bar

Start it, `curl` the model endpoint, `PATCH` a column type, and show the
resulting `git diff` in the model directory. Then attempt a traversal write and
paste the refusal.

## Out of scope

The canvas (dbmd-31), the inspector (dbmd-32), the watcher (dbmd-33).

title: dbmd check
description:
`dbmd check`: validate the model, print diagnostics, exit non-zero on error.

The command a team puts in CI so the model in the repository cannot drift into
something that does not parse.

## Scope

- Reads the model, runs `validate`, prints diagnostics grouped by file.
- Exit 0 when there are no errors, 1 when there are. `--strict` makes warnings
  errors.
- Plain text by default. `--json` emits the diagnostics as JSON for anyone
  wiring it into something else.

## Watch out for

- A parse failure is an error, not a crash. `dbmd check` on a repository with
  one broken file must report that file and still report on all the rest.
- Exit codes are the whole contract in CI. Test them, and test that `--json`
  still exits non-zero rather than exiting 0 because printing succeeded.

## Evidence bar

Run it in a directory with one broken file and one dangling ref, and paste both
the output and the exit code you actually observed.

title: CLI entry point and dbmd init
description:
The CLI entry point, and `dbmd init`.

## Scope

- `src/cli.ts` with a shebang, wired as the package `bin` named `dbmd`.
- Argument parsing with no dependency: the surface is four commands and a
  handful of flags, and `parseArgs` from `node:util` is in the standard library.
- `dbmd init [dir]` creates the model directory with `_model.md` and one example
  table demonstrating the format, including prose and a `ref`. It refuses to
  overwrite an existing non-empty directory.
- `--help` on the root and on each command. `--version` from package.json.
- Unknown command and unknown flag both exit non-zero with a message naming what
  was expected.

## Watch out for

- `npx` runs this on Windows. Path handling goes through `node:path`, and the
  shebang plus the `bin` mapping is what makes it run at all. Test from a
  `npm pack` tarball rather than from the source tree: the source tree hides a
  missing `files` entry, and that failure only appears for your users.
- The example model `init` writes is the first thing every user reads. It is
  documentation, not a fixture. Make it a small, real-looking schema.

## Evidence bar

`npm pack`, install the tarball into an empty temporary directory, run
`npx dbmd init` there, and paste the files it produced. Not `node src/cli.ts`.

## Out of scope

`check`, `export` and `studio` are their own items.

title: Validation with actionable diagnostics
description:
Validate a model and produce diagnostics a human can act on.

## Scope

`src/model/validate.ts`: a `validate(model)` returning diagnostics, each with a
severity, a message, the file path and, where it can be known honestly, a line
number.

The rules for the MVP:

- every ref resolves to a table and a column that exist
- no two tables share a name; no two columns in a table share a name
- no two indexes in a table share a name
- an index names only columns that exist in its table
- a table with no primary key is a warning, not an error
- a ref whose target is neither unique nor a primary key is a warning: it is
  usually a typo and occasionally deliberate
- a group key naming a group that does not exist is an error
- a group with no members is a warning: an empty group is almost always a rename
  that went wrong
- a file whose kind disagrees with its directory is an error

## Watch out for

- A line number that is wrong is worse than no line number. If you cannot derive
  one honestly from the parse, omit it. Do not guess by searching the file for
  the column name: a column named `id` appears forty times.
- Warnings must not fail `dbmd check` by default, or nobody will put it in CI.
  Errors fail; warnings print. `--strict` promotes warnings, and that flag is
  what a team opts into.
- Diagnostics are output, so ADR 0006 applies: they sort deterministically, and
  the JSON shape is a contract before it is a convenience.

## Evidence bar

Run it against a fixture with a dangling ref, a duplicate column, a missing
primary key, an empty group and a misfiled note, and paste the exact terminal
output. It should be readable without the file open beside it.

## Out of scope

The `dbmd check` command that wraps this (dbmd-21).

title: Owner: the name, and whether this is published to npm
description:
Owner decision: the name, and whether this gets published to npm.

`dbmd` is a working name, chosen because it is short, says what it does, and was
unclaimed on npm on 2026-08-24. Nothing depends on it being the final name yet,
and that stops being true the moment dbmd-50 lands and a README says it.

## What is needed

1. Is `dbmd` the name? If not, what is, and it should be checked on npm before
   it goes into files.
2. Is this published publicly to npm, or installed from a git URL inside your
   own projects? `npx` works from a git URL, so publishing is not required for
   the workflow to work.
3. If public: scoped (`@blakehastings/dbmd`) or unscoped?

## Recommendation

Keep `dbmd` and publish unscoped. It costs nothing to hold the name now, and
`npx dbmd studio` is the sentence the whole tool is trying to be. The cost of
being wrong is a rename before anyone depends on it, which is cheap.

## Meanwhile

Everything proceeds under the working name. The rename would touch package.json,
the bin name and the README, and nothing else, because no source file should
hardcode it.
close_reason: Answered: the name is dbmd, MIT licensed, public on GitHub. LICENSE and package metadata landed in the same pass.

comments.author: Blake Hastings
comments.text:
Answered by the owner on 2026-08-24.

- The name is `dbmd`. It was free on npm when checked the same day.
- It goes on GitHub as an open source project, MIT licensed.
- Public repository, unscoped package.

Acted on in the same pass: LICENSE added, package.json carries the licence,
repository, homepage and bugs fields, and the repository was created and pushed.

Publishing to npm itself is still a separate step and has not happened. dbmd-50
is what makes the package correct enough for it.

title: The studio
description:
The local web editor, as ADR 0004 describes it: a view onto files, not a diagram
application that imports and exports them.

The files are the state. Every edit writes through to disk, there is no Save
button, and undo is `git checkout`. The client is vanilla TypeScript and SVG
bundled with esbuild; there is no UI framework and no diagram library, and ADR
0004 says why and when to revisit that.

Read `docs/architecture/decisions/0004-the-studio-is-a-local-editor-of-files.md`
before opening any child of this epic.

title: The command line
description:
The command line surface. Four commands in the MVP:

- `dbmd init` scaffolds a model directory
- `dbmd check` validates and exits non-zero, for CI
- `dbmd studio` opens the local editor (epic dbmd-3)
- `dbmd export` writes a mermaid diagram other people can read on GitHub

The tool is run with `npx`, so start-up time and install size are features, not
afterthoughts. Anything that costs a dependency has to say what it buys.

title: The SQL Server provider
description:
The SQL Server provider.

Read `docs/architecture/decisions/0007-engines-are-providers.md` and
`docs/import-format.md` from dbmd-40 first. This is the item that proves the
seam was real rather than Postgres wearing an interface, so a change forced into
`contract.ts` here is a finding worth reporting, not a nuisance.

## Scope

- `src/import/providers/sqlserver.ts` implementing `EngineProvider`.
- One statement, printed by `dbmd query --engine sqlserver`, returning the
  envelope as JSON via `FOR JSON PATH`.
- `parse` and `normaliseType`, plus `[bracket]` quoting.
- A committed fixture and unit tests over it.

## Watch out for

- **SSMS splits `FOR JSON` output across rows at about 2000 characters.** A user
  copying the grid gets truncated JSON that looks complete and fails to parse
  somewhere in the middle. This is the single most likely support question this
  feature will ever generate. Say so in the printed output above the query, not
  only in the documentation, and make the parse failure name it as a likely
  cause.
- `FOR JSON` needs SQL Server 2016 or later. Say what happens on older versions
  rather than producing a syntax error nobody can interpret.
- `nvarchar(max)` reports `max_length` as -1, and `nvarchar` reports bytes rather
  than characters, so a `nvarchar(50)` reads as 100.
- `sys.indexes`, `sys.index_columns` and `sys.foreign_key_columns` carry what
  `information_schema` does not, including included columns and whether an index
  is the clustered one.
- Default constraints arrive wrapped in extra parentheses, `((0))` for zero.
  Decide whether to unwrap and be consistent.
- Collation is case-insensitive by default, so two tables differing only in case
  cannot normally exist. Do not build that assumption into the contract, and do
  not build the opposite one either.
- `dbo` is the default schema and is not the same as "no schema".

## Evidence bar

Run it against a real SQL Server, on a schema with a composite primary key, a
multi-column foreign key, an `nvarchar(max)` column and a non-`dbo` schema.
Paste the JSON, and say which SQL Server version and which client you used. If
no instance is available, say so plainly rather than inventing output, and say
what that leaves unproven.

Separately, and this is the architectural part: report every change this item
forced on `contract.ts` or on `EngineProvider`. That list is the measure of
whether ADR 0007's seam was in the right place.

comments.author: Blake Hastings
comments.text:
Resolved ahead of this item by dbmd-40, which merged the contract first.

This item's brief says "default constraints arrive wrapped in extra
parentheses, `((0))` for zero. Decide whether to unwrap and be consistent."
That decision has now been taken the other way: the contract stores default
expressions **verbatim**, `((0))` included, and `docs/import-format.md` says so.

So this item does not decide it. If the SQL Server provider has a reason to
disagree, the change is to the format doc and the contract, argued in the pull
request, not an unwrap inside the provider. A provider that quietly normalises
what the contract says is verbatim is the exact drift the seam exists to stop.

One other thing settled since this was written: `EngineProvider.normaliseType`
returns the closed `NormalisedType` union rather than ADR 0007's `string`, with
`other` as the escape hatch. ADR 0009 has the argument.

title: The Postgres provider
description:
The Postgres provider.

Read `docs/architecture/decisions/0007-engines-are-providers.md` and
`docs/import-format.md` from dbmd-40 first.

## Scope

- `src/import/providers/postgres.ts` implementing `EngineProvider`.
- One SQL statement, printed by `dbmd query --engine postgres`, returning one
  JSON value in the envelope shape.
- `parse` and `normaliseType` turning that into the canonical shape.
- A committed fixture of real output, and unit tests over it that need no
  database.

## Watch out for

- One statement. No psql meta-commands, no temporary tables, no `\gset`. It has
  to paste into pgAdmin, DBeaver, a JDBC console and `docker exec psql` alike.
- **Read-only, and visibly so.** Somebody is going to run this against
  production, and they should be able to satisfy themselves by reading it. Do not
  make that hard to see.
- Exclude `pg_catalog` and `information_schema` from the results, or the first
  import produces four hundred tables.
- `information_schema` does not carry usable index metadata. `pg_index`,
  `pg_class` and `pg_attribute` do. It is also materially slower on large
  catalogs.
- Identity columns and `serial` produce different defaults for the same intent.
  Decide what the model should say and be consistent.
- Case. Postgres folds unquoted identifiers to lower case, so a table created as
  `"Orders"` is a different table from `Orders`. The JSON must carry what is
  actually there, not what somebody typed.

## Evidence bar

Run it against a real Postgres, on a schema with at least one composite primary
key, one multi-column foreign key, and one quoted mixed-case identifier. Paste
the JSON. If no database is available, say so plainly and do not substitute a
schema you invented: a fixture proves the normalisation and never the query, and
that distinction is in ADR 0007.

title: The GitHub Actions recipe: check, and publish the diagram
description:
The GitHub Actions recipe: check the model, and publish the diagram.

The pipeline caller from ADR 0006, made concrete. Two jobs a team would actually
want, documented well enough to copy.

## Scope

- A documented workflow snippet that runs `dbmd check` on a repository's model
  and fails the build on an error.
- A second that runs `dbmd export` and uploads the result as a build artifact,
  so a pull request can carry the current diagram without anyone committing a
  generated file if they would rather not.
- Both in the README or a `docs/ci.md`, as copy-paste YAML with the version
  pinned, not as prose describing what you could do.
- This repository uses its own recipe on `examples/shop`, which is how it stays
  true.

## Watch out for

- `npx dbmd@latest` in someone's CI is a supply chain decision made by accident.
  Pin a version in the recipe and say why.
- No TTY, so anything that assumed one shows up here first. This item is the
  real test of dbmd-70 and should be treated as such.
- An artifact upload that silently uploads nothing when the export produced
  nothing is worse than a failure. Make the export's exit code meaningful.

## Evidence bar

The workflow runs in this repository, on a real push, and goes green. Link the
run and paste the artifact's contents. A YAML file that has never executed is
not evidence.

title: Publishable package, verified from a tarball
description:
Make the package installable and `npx`-able.

## Scope

- `bin`, `files`, `exports`, `engines` set correctly. Drop `private: true`.
- The client bundle is built before pack and included in the tarball.
- `prepublishOnly` runs `npm run check`.
- A smoke test that packs the tarball, installs it into a temporary directory
  and runs `dbmd --version` and `dbmd init`, wired into `npm run check` if it is
  fast enough and into its own script if it is not.

## Watch out for

- `files` omissions are invisible locally and fatal for users. The source tree
  has everything; the tarball is what ships. Test the tarball.
- The shebang must survive the build, and the built file needs to be executable
  on a POSIX install even though it is produced on Windows.
- `npx dbmd` on a machine with no cache downloads the tarball. Every dependency
  is start-up latency for a first-time user; check the packed size and say what
  it is in the pull request.

## Evidence bar

From a directory outside this repository, install the packed tarball and run
`npx dbmd init` and `npx dbmd studio`. Paste both, and the packed size.

title: The README a stranger reads
description:
The README a stranger reads.

## Scope

- The workflow, in the order a real user meets it: install nothing, run
  `npx dbmd init` or `npx dbmd import`, run `npx dbmd studio`, edit, `git diff`,
  commit, pull request.
- One screenshot of the studio and one real markdown file, side by side. That
  pairing is the whole product and no paragraph explains it as well.
- What it is not: not a migration tool, not a database client, does not connect
  to anything.
- A link to the format documentation and to ADR 0003.

## Watch out for

- The README currently claims a status that will be wrong the moment this
  lands. Do not leave a status line that quietly becomes a lie.
- Do not write the README from the ADRs. Write it from having run the tool, and
  paste what you actually saw.

title: dbmd import into an empty model
description:
`dbmd import`: turn the introspection JSON into a model directory.

## Scope

- `dbmd import --file schema.json [--dir db-model]`, and reading stdin when no
  file is given, so a pipe works.
- Writes one markdown file per table, through the canonical writer (dbmd-11).
- Tables are laid out on a deterministic grid. There is no auto layout in the
  MVP and the developer arranges them once.
- Refuses to write into a non-empty model directory. The message names dbmd-42
  as the merge that does not exist yet, so the user knows the difference between
  unimplemented and forbidden.
- The generated prose body is a single line saying the table was imported and
  nobody has documented it yet. That is a prompt, and it is the point.

## Watch out for

- Do not invent prose. An imported model with a paragraph of generated
  description per table teaches the reader that the prose is worthless, which
  destroys the one thing this format has that a diagram does not.
- Types come back from Postgres as things like `character varying` and
  `timestamp with time zone`. Decide once whether to normalise them and say so
  in the pull request; whichever you choose, be consistent, because this is what
  every user's first diff looks like.
- A foreign key with no matching table in the JSON is a bad export, not a bad
  model. Diagnose it, do not write a dangling ref silently.

## Evidence bar

Import the fixture from dbmd-40 and paste `dbmd check` output on the result: it
should be clean. Then open the studio on it and include a screenshot.

title: The introspection contract and the provider seam
description:
The introspection contract and the provider seam. No engine.

The first of three: this item defines the shape and the registry, dbmd-43 is
Postgres and dbmd-44 is SQL Server. Doing the seam first is deliberate. A
contract extracted from one working engine is that engine wearing an interface.

Read `docs/architecture/decisions/0007-engines-are-providers.md` first.

## Scope

- `src/import/contract.ts`: the canonical introspection shape, as types plus a
  validator. It is the **union** of what Postgres and SQL Server can say, not
  the intersection and not Postgres with room bolted on the side. Composite
  primary keys, multi-column foreign keys, schemas and index metadata are all in
  it because both engines have them.
- The envelope: `{ dbmdIntrospection: 1, engine: "...", ... }`, so a pasted file
  says what produced it and `dbmd import` cannot be handed the wrong provider.
- `src/import/providers/index.ts`: the registry. Adding an engine is one file
  and one line here, and nothing outside this directory learns an engine's name.
- `EngineProvider` as ADR 0007 declares it: `introspectionQuery`, `parse`,
  `normaliseType`, `quoteIdentifier`.
- `docs/import-format.md`: the contract as documentation, with a worked example.
  This is what somebody writing the third provider reads.
- A deliberately fake provider in the tests, so the registry and the envelope
  dispatch are tested without either real engine.

## Watch out for

- Designing this from Postgres alone. Open the SQL Server catalog before fixing
  the shape: `nvarchar(max)` reporting length -1, and `sys.*` carrying index
  information that `information_schema` does not, are both things that change
  what the contract needs to hold.
- A normalised type vocabulary that silently loses information. Decide now
  whether the native type string is kept alongside the normalised one. ADR 0007
  flags this as a revisit trigger, which means it is cheaper to get right here.
- The version number is not decoration. Write the code path that rejects an
  unknown `dbmdIntrospection` with a message naming the version it got and the
  version it wanted, and test it, or the field is a comment.

## Evidence bar

Two hand-written fixture files, one shaped like each engine's output, and the
fake provider resolving both through the registry from the envelope alone. Paste
the diagnostic produced by a file with an unknown version and by a file with an
unknown engine.

## Out of scope

Any real SQL. That is dbmd-43 and dbmd-44.
close_reason: Merged in PR #6. Contract verified bi-engine by driving it: -1 length rejected, max accepted, empty schema rejected, explicit nulls stripped so null and absent are identical.

comments.author: Blake Hastings
comments.text:
Marked blocked by dbmd-91 rather than briefed to assume Postgres.

The JSON contract is reusable across engines but the query itself is not, so a
wrong guess here throws the whole item away rather than costing an assumption.
That is the "refuse to start work whose inputs are missing" case, not the "state
your assumption and carry on" case.

comments.author: Blake Hastings
comments.text:
## Functionality

Drove the contract myself against documents I wrote, not the fixtures in the PR.
Compiled `dist` and called `validateIntrospectionDocument` and
`readIntrospection` directly.

The claim this item lives or dies on is that the shape is genuinely the union of
two engines rather than Postgres with room bolted on. Checked the SQL Server
half specifically, because that is the half that cannot be reached by
imagination:

- `length: -1` is rejected, and the message names why it exists:
  ``` `length` must be a non-negative whole number or the string "max", got -1;
  SQL Server reports -1 for the max forms and a provider translates that here ```
- `length: "max"` is accepted with no diagnostics.
- `schema: ""` is rejected. `dbo` being a schema name rather than "no schema" is
  enforced, not just documented.
- Explicit `null` on `comment`, `default`, `identity`, `collation` and
  `primaryKey` produces no diagnostics and the nulls are **stripped** from the
  validated value, so null and absent really are the same thing. That is the
  `FOR JSON` behaviour the report claims, and it is the one that a
  Postgres-first design would have got wrong by making null significant.
- Version 0, version 7 and an unknown engine produce the exact diagnostics
  reported, including the "this build has no engine providers at all" branch,
  which is `main`'s honest state today.

Verified independently: this is a bi-engine contract.

## Code

**The seam is real, and one claim in the report is understated rather than
overstated.** The report says `contract.ts` contains no engine name. It contains
twenty-one, and all of them are in comments and one diagnostic message,
explaining *which engine each field exists for*. None is in logic. That is
better than the claim, not worse: a field like `generated.persisted` is
incomprehensible without the sentence saying Postgres generated columns are
always stored. Leave them in.

`engineProviders` is an empty array on `main` with the one-import-one-line
pattern shown directly above it, and the empty-registry path has its own test.
A registry that is honestly empty beats one pre-seeded with providers that do
not exist yet.

`normaliseType` returning the closed `NormalisedType` union instead of ADR
0007's `string` is a deviation from a written interface, and it was reported
rather than slipped in. It is also the right call: an open return type cannot
be switched on, which is the only reason a normalised name exists at all, and
`other` is the escape hatch. ADR 0009 records it against 0007 explicitly, so
the next reader does not have to work out which document is wrong.

## Architecture

ADR 0009 settles the question ADR 0007 left open, and settles it on the argument
that matters: the asymmetry is recovery. A model written without the native type
cannot get it back without a re-import against a database the user may no longer
have, so keeping both is the choice that cannot be regretted.

Three of the four assumptions are the right kind. Check constraints being in the
contract, unnamed by this item, is justified by the alternative being a contract
change during dbmd-43. The `--engine` override landing as a warning before the
flag exists is the kind of thing that is normally scope creep and here it is
what stops dbmd-41 reaching past the seam.

What it hands the two provider items is stated as a list of things they will
have to fight, including that expressions stay verbatim and `((0))` is not
unwrapped. dbmd-44's brief says "decide whether to unwrap"; the contract has
decided. That is a contradiction between an open item and a merged decision, and
it is resolved the right way round: if dbmd-44 disagrees it changes the format
doc rather than unwrapping quietly. I will update dbmd-44 to say so.

## Verdict

Merge. No changes requested.

title: Watch the directory, survive a broken file
description:
Watch the model directory and reload, and show parse failures without dying.

This is what makes hand editing and studio editing the same feature seen from
two sides.

## Scope

- Watch the model directory. A file changing on disk updates the open studio.
- A file that fails to parse shows as an error on that table. The canvas keeps
  showing the last good version of it rather than emptying.
- Writes the studio itself made must not bounce back as an external change.

## Watch out for

- An editor saving a file produces several filesystem events, and often a
  temporary file and a rename rather than a write. Debounce and re-read from
  disk rather than trusting the event.
- The echo. The studio writes, the watcher fires, the studio reloads, and if the
  reload is not identical you have a loop that rewrites the file forever. Ignore
  a change whose content matches what you just wrote.
- `fs.watch` is not consistent across platforms and this project runs on
  Windows. Verify on Windows specifically, not on the assumption that it behaves
  like a mac.

## Evidence bar

With the studio open, edit a table file in an editor and confirm the canvas
updates. Then break the YAML in that file and paste a screenshot of what the
studio shows. Then fix it and confirm it recovers without a restart.

title: dbmd export to mermaid
description:
`dbmd export --format mermaid`: a diagram other people can read on GitHub.

The cheapest possible answer to "so other devs can see", and it works inside a
pull request without anyone installing anything, because GitHub renders mermaid
in markdown.

## Scope

- Writes `db-model/README.md` containing a mermaid `erDiagram` block generated
  from the model, between markers, so the rest of that file stays a place for
  humans to write.
- `--stdout` prints instead of writing.
- Deterministic output: same model, same bytes. Sort tables and relationships.

## Watch out for

- Mermaid's ER syntax is fussy about names. A table or column with a space, a
  hyphen or a reserved word breaks the whole diagram, and the failure is a blank
  box on GitHub rather than an error anywhere you will see it. Escape or quote,
  and put a table named `order-items` in the fixture.
- A large model produces an unreadable diagram. That is acceptable, and worth
  one sentence in the generated file rather than a layout algorithm.
- Regenerating must not disturb prose outside the markers, and must not rewrite
  the file at all when the diagram has not changed.

## Evidence bar

Paste the generated block, and confirm you viewed it rendered rather than
reading the source. A markdown preview that renders mermaid is enough.

title: Owner: which database engines the import must cover
description:
Owner decision: which database engines the import has to cover.

dbmd-40 builds the Postgres introspection query on the assumption that Postgres
is the one that matters first. That assumption is not derivable from anything in
this repository.

## What is needed

Which engines do the applications you would point this at actually use, in
order? Postgres, MySQL or MariaDB, SQL Server, SQLite, something else.

## Why it matters now rather than later

The JSON contract in dbmd-40 is designed once. A contract shaped by one engine
grows warts when the second arrives, and the two that would shape it most
differently are SQL Server, whose schema and identifier rules do not match
Postgres, and SQLite, which has no information schema at all.

Naming the second engine now costs an hour of design in dbmd-40. Discovering it
after dbmd-41 costs a rewrite of both.

## Recommendation

Postgres first, and tell me the second one even if it is months away. If the
answer is genuinely "only Postgres", say so and the contract gets simpler.

## Meanwhile

dbmd-40 proceeds on Postgres and is briefed to keep the JSON shape engine
neutral where that is free, which is most of it.
close_reason: Answered: Postgres and SQL Server, behind a provider seam. ADR 0007, and dbmd-40 split into 40, 43 and 44.

comments.author: Blake Hastings
comments.text:
Answered by the owner on 2026-08-25: Postgres and SQL Server for now, with a
proper provider pattern so a third engine is additive rather than a rewrite.

Recorded as ADR 0007. Two engines chosen up front is the number that forces the
design: one lets you call a single query an architecture, and three would be a
rewrite of whatever one produced.

dbmd-40 is rewritten as the contract and the provider seam with no engine in it,
and split from dbmd-43 (Postgres) and dbmd-44 (SQL Server). The seam comes first
deliberately, because a contract extracted from one working engine is that
engine wearing an interface.

title: Import from a live database
description:
Bootstrap a model from a database that already exists.

The shape is deliberately borrowed from ChartDB and it is the best idea in that
product: the tool never connects to the database and never asks for credentials.
It prints a query, the developer runs it themselves with whatever client they
already trust, and hands back the JSON it produced.

That keeps database drivers out of the dependency tree, keeps secrets out of the
tool entirely, and works through a bastion host or a VPN without any of it being
our problem.

title: Publishable as npx dbmd
description:
Make `npx dbmd` work for somebody who has never seen this repository.

Publishing to npm is the owner's step and is not something the loop does on its
own. What this epic covers is everything up to that: the package being correct,
the binary resolving, the bundle being present in the tarball, and a README that
shows the real workflow rather than an aspiration.

title: probe
close_reason: Probe of explicit ids. They work, so the backlog uses readable sequential ids rather than hashes.

title: Re-import without losing prose or layout
description:
Re-import over an existing model without losing what humans wrote.

The feature that turns import from a one-time bootstrap into something a team
runs every release. It is also the item most likely to be wrong in a way nobody
notices until prose is gone, which is why it is separate from dbmd-41.

Not dispatchable yet: the merge rules are a conversation, not a derivation. What
happens to a table that disappeared from the database, a column that changed
type, and a column that was removed and whose prose mentions it are three
different decisions and all three are the owner's.

## Sketch, to be settled in refinement

- Match by table name, then by column name.
- Prose bodies and `layout` always survive.
- A table in the model but not in the database is reported, not deleted.
- Changes are shown before they are written, or written and left for `git diff`.

title: A skill that teaches an agent to drive dbmd
description:
A skill that teaches an agent to drive dbmd.

Not dispatchable. Filed so the MVP does not close the door on it, and so the
question is on the record rather than in a conversation.

## What has to be true first

The MVP exists and somebody has used it by hand for long enough to know what the
awkward parts are. Designing an agent interface before that is inventing an
interface for a user nobody has met.

## The questions refinement has to answer

- Does the agent go through the CLI, or does it edit markdown directly? Directly
  is easier and wrong: it bypasses the validator and the canonical writer, which
  is exactly how you get the churning diffs this format exists to prevent.
- Is there a command an agent needs that a human does not? Adding a column from
  a description, for instance, or answering "what points at this table".
- What does the agent do when `dbmd check` fails on its own edit? Reverting is
  one answer and reporting is another, and they are different products.
- Where does the skill live: in this repository, published alongside the package,
  or both?

## What already points this way and should stay pointed

ADR 0006's JSON contract, deterministic output, `dbmd check` as the feedback
signal, and the prose body being preserved byte for byte, which is what stops an
agent quietly reflowing something a human wrote.

title: An agent can drive the model
description:
An agent can drive the model.

Deliberately after the MVP, and filed now so the design does not accidentally
close the door on it.

The shape: a skill that teaches an agent how to read and change a dbmd model
without opening the studio. An agent editing markdown files directly is already
possible and is the wrong default, because it bypasses the validator and the
canonical writer, and produces exactly the churning diffs the format exists to
prevent. The skill's job is to route that through the CLI instead.

What already points this way and should stay pointed:

- ADR 0006's JSON contract, so an agent never parses prose
- deterministic output, so an agent never chases a diff that is only sort order
- `dbmd check`, which is how an agent finds out it broke something
- the prose body being preserved byte for byte, which is what stops an agent
  quietly reflowing a human's paragraph

Nothing here is dispatchable until the MVP exists and somebody has driven the
tool by hand enough to know what an agent would want. Refining this before that
would be inventing an interface for a user nobody has met.
